evals.name: pe-botrytis-night
evals.prompt: We grow tomatoes in a glass greenhouse in the Netherlands. It's March and we're getting Botrytis in the plant heads and water droplets on the lower fruits in the morning. At night we run a 45 C minimum pipe temperature and keep our energy screen 95% closed with a 5% gap to get rid of humidity. Night RH is around 90%. What should we change?
assertions: Identifies heat emission / plant heads or fruits cooling below dew point as the cause of free water, not just high RH
Recommends closing the screen fully (no moisture gap) or a double screen, explaining that gaps drop cold air and create cold spots
Recommends removing moisture by condensation on the roof and/or ventilating above the closed screen instead of gapping
Recommends replacing or lowering the minimum pipe temperature and using fans (preferably vertical) for air movement
Addresses morning condensation on fruits: raise temperature gradually before sunrise and/or keep the screen closed until the air above it has warmed
Recommends monitoring absolute humidity / dew point versus crop temperature (e.g. aspirator box above the screen, leaf or fruit temperature)

evals.name: pe-sunny-wilting
evals.prompt: Our cucumbers wilt around noon on sunny summer days. We open the roof vents wide once the greenhouse reaches 24 C and we dose CO2. Leaves feel warm to the touch and RH drops to about 50%. Should we put on whitewash or close the shade screen?
assertions: Warns that shading/whitewash cuts photosynthesis and can start a negative spiral, and advises trying humidity and water-supply measures first
Recommends ventilating less / allowing a higher temperature (e.g. 26-28 C) to keep humidity and CO2 inside on sunny days
Explains that evaporation is driven by absorbed energy (radiation) rather than by low RH, and that warm leaves indicate closing stomata / water stress
Recommends measuring leaf temperature and/or VPD, with roughly 0.3-1.5 kPa as healthy and above ~1.5 kPa as stress
Addresses water supply or root uptake (e.g. irrigation based on radiation, ramping up in the morning, root health)
Mentions misting or another way to raise RH under high radiation, and/or the CO2 lost through wide-open vents

evals.name: pe-rtr-setpoints
evals.prompt: Can you explain RTR and how we'd actually use it to set day and night temperatures for our tomato crop? We have outdoor radiation data in J/cm2 from our weather station.
assertions: Defines RTR as the ratio of 24-hour average temperature to the daily light (radiation/PAR) sum
Describes plotting each day as a point (light sum vs average temperature) and following a target line
Explains the too-strong/vegetative (more light, same temperature) vs too-weak/generative (higher temperature, little light) logic
Gives the day-to-day practice: after a sunny day keep the night warmer or postpone the drop, after a dark day keep the night cooler
Links RTR to plant load planned against the expected (long-term average) light curve, noting a lower load allows a higher temperature per unit light
Notes preconditions or corrections: CO2/RH not limiting, and PAR at crop level is better than outdoor radiation when whitewash/screens cut light
